item.title: All-you-can-eat dining makes a comeback as Americans look for more bang for their buck
item.description: From Southern comfort food to Uzbek hot bars and Korean BBQ, these five all-you-can-eat buffet spots are fueling a massive U.S. dining trend.
item.content:encoded:
With grocery and restaurant prices climbing, Americans have a hearty appetite for all-you-can-eat and buffet-style dining.

Yelp searches for all-you-can-eat buffets jumped 252% from 2025, The Wall Street Journal recently reported.

While major chains like Golden Corral often dominate the buffet landscape, the outlet highlighted five other spots offering everything from Southern comfort food and Uzbek specialties to Korean barbecue and Brazilian steakhouse fare. 

AMERICA'S BIGGEST BUFFET CHAIN CRACKED THE CODE TO ALL-YOU-CAN-EAT PROFITS

Here they are below:

Since opening in September, Good Time has brought Southern-style comfort food to Manhattan, with dishes such as Salisbury steak, collard greens, dinner rolls and peach cobbler.

Unlimited servings cost $26.99, according to the Journal. Co-founder David Yun said the goal was to offer "something affordable" and evoke "the humble buffet that really brings you back to that memory."

DOLLY PARTON'S FAVORITE SOUTHERN DISHES, FROM CHICKEN AND DUMPLINGS TO BANANA PUDDING

Tashkent's Uzbek hot bar, also in New York City, features dozens of prepared dishes, including plov, stuffed cabbage, manti dumplings and pastries. 

Customers pay by weight, unlike the all-you-can-eat buffets. The Journal reported that takeout containers typically cost $10.99 to $11.99 per pound.

GROCERY STORE SWITCH COULD SAVE AMERICANS MONEY WHILE SHAKING UP DINNER ROUTINES

Since opening last year, Tashkent's West Village location has put a spotlight on Central Asian cuisine, with food bloggers helping to draw attention to its hot bar, The Guardian reported.

KPot Korean BBQ and Hot Pot lets diners cook meats, vegetables and noodles at the table, barbecue-style or in hot broth. 

For $5 extra, diners can do both, The Journal reported, noting that prices vary, from $36.99 in New York to $31.99 in Oklahoma City.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

With locations in nearly 40 states, KPot is one of the largest Korean restaurant chains in the country.

Der Dutchman serves hearty, Amish- and Mennonite-inspired fare, including creamed chicken, meatloaf, baked ham and noodles with mashed potatoes. 

It is among several famous heartland spots that often land on the country's best buffets lists and has "a good rocking-chair-on-a-big-front-porch type of vibe," one diner told the Journal.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

All-you-can-eat dinners cost about $20 for adults, while breakfast was about $14 and included pancakes, biscuits and regional specialties such as tomato gravy and fried cornmeal mush, according to the outlet.

Fogo de Chão offers two distinct lunch options: an unlimited Market Table with soups, salads, breads and Brazilian specialties, and the Full Churrasco Experience, which adds fire-roasted meats served at the table. 

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The Journal reported the Market Table at $20, with the full meat service costing about $30 more. Availability and prices can vary by location.

The Brazilian steakhouse is a hit among Gen Z and has almost doubled its footprint to nearly 115 locations in the U.S. in the last four years, according to the Journal.

item.title: Trump ‘holds all the cards’ in war against Iran’s regime, White House says
item.description: Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei taunts America after midterms, but the White House says Trump holds all the cards on the Strait of Hormuz.
item.content:encoded:
JERUSALEM — With Iran’s missing-in-action Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei taunting Americans about the "collapse" of the U.S. after the midterm elections, the White House and Middle East experts argue Trump is positioned to defeat the remnants of the rogue regime.

The remaining two years of President Trump’s Iran policy have profound implications for his legacy and could lay the foundation for a new Middle East devoid of the region’s worst state sponsor of terrorism, the Islamic Republic of Iran, should Trump pursue new military actions to dislodge Khamenei’s regime, according to experts.

Khamenei, who has not been seen in public since a joint U.S.-Israel airstrike killed his father, former Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, and members of his family, boasted on X following the Republican defeat in the midterms: "The process of the US's collapse has accelerated."

IRAN TAKES A VICTORY LAP OVER STUNNING US ELECTION RESULTS, CLAIMS 'COLLAPSE HAS ACCELERATED'

The radical Islamist clerical ruler’s braggadocio was met with tough statements from the White House and leading Middle East experts on Iran’s theocratic state.

A White House spokesperson told Fox News Digital that "The United States is in a very strong position with control of the Strait of Hormuz and the Iranian economy collapsing. Iran has been decimated, and things will go one of two ways; the easy way or the hard way. President Trump holds all the cards and will do whatever is best for the United States."

TRUMP REVIVES IRAN REGIME CHANGE SPECULATION WITH CRYPTIC CALL FOR PEOPLE TO 'RISE UP'

The spokesperson added, "Only President Trump knows what he will do and when."

The Islamic Republic ramped up its bellicose anti-American and anti-Western rhetoric and activities over the last week. Tehran presented a "Trump in a Cage" exhibit with a mock execution of Trump to coincide with the regime’s anniversary of its illegal seizure of the U.S. Embassy and kidnapping of its personnel on Nov. 4, 1979.

TRUMP CALLS IRAN CONFLICT A 'SOFT WAR,' INSISTS US HOLDS THE CARDS AHEAD OF MIDTERM ELECTIONS

The Ayatollahs did not restrict their jingoism to the U.S. An AI-generated video published by state-controlled Iranian media outlets shows the spokesperson of the headquarters of the Islamic Republic of Iran Armed Forces threatening Western Europe. The spokesperson said, "We are not like you. Iran does not harm innocents. You are not our enemy. But anyone, anywhere in Europe, who assists America in harming our women and children is our enemy, and we will punish them."

The video features military targets in France, Germany and Britain.

Navid Mohebbi, who worked as a Persian media analyst for the State Department's Public Affairs Bureau, told Fox News Digital, "Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, went so far as to claim that Iran had inflicted a political defeat on Trump in Washington, in addition to its supposed victories on the battlefield and in the Strait of Hormuz. Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf similarly portrayed the election results as an American rejection of the war."

TRUMP CAN’T LET IRAN TURN A MILITARY DEFEAT TURN INTO A DIPLOMATIC VICTORY

He added that "This is part of a broader psychological and political campaign. Tehran, along with commentators sympathetic to the regime in the United States, is trying to promote the wildly exaggerated narrative that confronting the Islamic Republic carries an unbearable electoral cost for American politicians."

Mohebbi said the "evidence does not support the claim that the Iran war alone caused the Republican defeat. According to national exit polling, only 4% of voters identified foreign policy as the country’s single most important issue."

The phrase "finish the job" has become synonymous with toppling the 47-year ironclad totalitarian rule of the Islamic Republic.

IRAN’S REGIME WON’T NEGOTIATE IN GOOD FAITH. TRUMP MUST BREAK ITS GRIP

"I believe President Trump should finish the job, because the fundamental threats posed by the Islamic Republic remain unresolved," Mohebbi said, adding, "The nuclear file is far from closed. Iran’s highly enriched uranium stockpile remains unaccounted for under international verification, and the regime has retained the ability to rebuild elements of its ballistic missile program. More importantly, its underlying strategic behavior and hostility toward the United States and its regional allies have not fundamentally changed."

Former Pentagon official Simone Ledeen told the London-based Iran International news organization the Islamic Republic "needs to end" and regime will never change its behavior. She called support for Iran’s people on the ground and opposes putting American troops on the ground.

TRUMP IS DISMANTLING IRAN’S WAR MACHINE, BUT AMERICA STILL NEEDS AN ENDGAME

Veteran Iran observers and experts have noted that President Trump was the first U.S. leader not to kick the Iran nuclear weapons problem down the road. His decision to confront Iran’s illegal atomic weapons system was one of the most decisive foreign policy achievements of his administration, according to popular American commentators like Ben Shapiro.

Shapiro termed Trump’s Operation Epic Fury campaign against Iran "the single bravest foreign policy move of my lifetime."

"What you’re watching him [Trump] do in Iran is not only unprecedented in terms of its political courage. I think that it is and has the potential to be a true game changer for America’s role in the world, not only for the next 10 or 20 years, but for the coming century," Shapiro told Lara Trump on Fox News' "My View" in March.

AFTER 47 YEARS OF CONFRONTING IRAN, DOES AMERICA HAVE A STRATEGY FOR ENDING THIS WAR?

Mohebbi said: "There is also a critical factor that Washington must understand: the Islamic Republic is attempting to wait out the Trump administration. Even if Trump were to negotiate the strongest possible agreement today, I believe Tehran would view it as a temporary arrangement rather than a permanent change in its strategic direction. The regime calculates that a future Democratic administration would not resort to military action against it. Once Tehran believes the threat of military force is off the table, it will become even more defiant in its behavior and more brazen at the negotiating table."

Another school of thought is to subcontract military actions to Israel against Iran’s regime.

IRAN REGIME CHANGE TALK RESURFACES AS TRUMP SAYS TEHRAN 'WANTS TO MEET' AMID US STRIKES

Mardo Soghom, an Iran expert who has written extensively about the Islamic Republic, told Fox News Digital that Tehran's strategy has always been to wait out U.S. pressure.

"They were hoping to ride out the Trump administration's pressures for two more years. Now they believe they have it," Soghom said. "I think he should give full support to Israel to do the job and not interfere. The U.S. should continue to maintain its blockade of Iran and facilitate shipping from the Persian Gulf, but except hitting well-protected and highly dangerous targets, such as nuclear sites if needed, the US should stay out of continuous attacks because its internal political situation is messed up."

Soghom, who tracks Iranian regime media, added the Iranian state radio is celebrating the Democratic victory.

"Incidentally, 47 years ago today, the new Islamic regime in Tehran gave the green light to its supporters to attack and seize the U.S. embassy," he said. "This election result will embolden them, and they'll not be inclined to compromise with the Trump admin — or even a future Democrat. Like in most other things, Trump did not finish the job when he could."

Jason Brodsky, policy director at United Against Nuclear Iran (UANI), told Fox News Digital that Iran sees the midterm election results as exacting a political cost from the Trump administration for launching Operation Epic Fury.

"It hopes these electoral losses will deter this and future administrations from launching military operations against Tehran over its aggression and terrorism," Brodsky said, adding that "At the same time, Iranian decision-makers are likely eyeing President Trump warily as U.S. presidents, even after midterm election losses, still have considerable discretion and authority as it relates to foreign policy. President Trump has proven unpredictable and, with over two years left in office, that is a lot of time for the U.S. to continue to damage the Iranian regime."

Brodsky noted that while Congress can complicate and raise objections, historically, without a veto-proof majority, it retains limited options for checking executive branch operations in this space.

"The 2006 midterm elections are instructive here, where, despite the prevailing anti-war sentiment at the time, President Bush still authorized a surge in the Iraq War," he said.

item.title: Stephen Colbert accused of crossing Harvard picket line before event with Yo-Yo Ma cut short by alarm
item.description: Stephen Colbert and Yo-Yo Ma are accused of crossing the Harvard Graduate Students Union picket line before a fire alarm cut their event short.
item.content:encoded:
Stephen Colbert, who publicly supported striking Hollywood writers in 2023, was accused of crossing a union picket line Thursday to join famed cellist Yo-Yo Ma at a Harvard University event that was abruptly cut short by a fire alarm.

Members of the Harvard Graduate Students Union, which has been on strike since Oct. 27, had urged Colbert and Ma to cancel, postpone or relocate the appearance in solidarity with workers seeking higher wages and stronger workplace protections. The union said it contacted both performers in advance, including through their respective labor organizations, but neither withdrew from the event.

The alarm sounded roughly 40 minutes into the sold-out event at Sanders Theatre, forcing Colbert, Ma and audience members to evacuate, according to Harvard Magazine. The discussion, titled "Arts for Life's Sake," had been scheduled to last 90 minutes but did not resume.

OBAMA FOUNDATION WORKERS MOVE TO UNIONIZE OVER BENEFITS, WORKING CONDITIONS MONTHS AFTER CENTER OPENS

About 50 union protesters demonstrated outside the theater before and during the event, beating drums, sounding air horns and chanting slogans demanding better pay and working conditions, the outlet reported.

The cause of the fire alarm remains unclear, and the union denied any involvement.

"The alarm was unrelated to HGSU's picketing activity and we have no knowledge of its cause," the union said in a social media statement, adding that members were relieved no one inside was at risk.

The union is seeking annual pay of $55,000 for research assistants and approximately $45,000 for teaching fellows on 10-month appointments, along with 3% annual raises or cost-of-living adjustments.

Other demands include an independent grievance process for harassment and discrimination complaints, legal fee assistance in Title IX cases and financial support for workers who need to leave unsafe laboratory environments.

The union is also seeking protections for sensitive immigration documents, guaranteed leave for visa delays or immigration emergencies, and a requirement that Harvard notify the union if Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents arrive on campus. It also wants the university to require a judicial warrant before cooperating with ICE.

The union had highlighted Colbert's support for the 2023 Writers Guild of America strike, during which he joined striking Hollywood workers on the picket line, in its appeal for the performers to reconsider their appearance.

FEDERAL JUDGE TOSSES TRUMP ADMIN HARVARD ADMISSIONS LAWSUIT, LEAVES DOOR OPEN TO FUTURE CHALLENGE

In a statement, the union said it had repeatedly urged Colbert and Ma to avoid crossing its picket line, including through their respective labor organizations, SAG-AFTRA and the Boston Musicians' Association.

"They continued the event inside without regard for the picket line, and refused to speak with union members as they left the event," the union said. "In other words — they crossed our picket line."

Author John Green, meanwhile, moved a scheduled Harvard appearance online to avoid crossing the graduate student union's picket line.

"They're on strike and I had to move a thing to not cross a picket line," Green said in a video shared by the union. "Which was an easy decision … it was not a hard decision for me."

Green also donated proceeds from the event to the union, according to The Boston Globe.

item.title: ROBERT L MAGINNIS: Iran War cost Republicans Congress. What will it cost America?
item.description: JD Vance blamed the Middle East conflict for Republican losses as Democrats flipped both houses of Congress after eight months of fighting Iran.
item.content:encoded:
Twenty years ago, American voters punished Republicans over an unpopular war in the Middle East. On Nov. 3, they did it again.

In 2006, it was Iraq. This time, it was Iran. Democrats captured both houses of Congress, flipping at least seven Senate seats, including Texas, Ohio, Kansas and Iowa. Vice President JD Vance put the blame squarely where President Donald Trump would rather not have it: on the war his administration launched eight months ago.

I remember the earlier debacle. As a Pentagon strategist during the run-up to the 2003 Iraq invasion, I attended meetings with Defense Secretary Donald Rumsfeld and senior military leaders. I questioned whether the administration had adequately considered what would follow Iraqi dictator Saddam Hussein’s overthrow.

HUGH HEWITT: THE GHOSTS OF 2006 ARE STIRRING — BUT WILL THEY CATCH THE GOP?

Now Trump faces a reckoning of his own. American forces have inflicted tremendous damage on Iran’s military. But military success does not guarantee strategic success, especially when the American people lose confidence in the mission.

Vance was blunt in his Nov. 4 assessment: "The reason we lost is the war." He dared anyone to argue that "losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it."

VANCE'S SCATHING IRAN WAR POSTMORTEM PUTS POTENTIAL 2028 GOP SHOWDOWN IN FOCUS: 'EVERYONE KNOWS WHY'

Trump acknowledged that the war contributed to Republican losses but defended his decision: "I would have done nothing differently." He added, "You can’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon."

He is right about that. But the election raises a question his administration has yet to answer: What has eight months of fighting accomplished that will last?

TRUMP IS DISMANTLING IRAN’S WAR MACHINE, BUT AMERICA STILL NEEDS AN ENDGAME

I have consistently argued that a nuclear-armed Iran is unacceptable. In June 2025, I supported decisive action against Tehran’s deeply buried Fordow nuclear facility. Four days later, however, I challenged claims that Iran was only weeks away from producing a usable nuclear weapon. The intelligence did not publicly establish that conclusion.

Those positions were consistent. Iran presented a serious threat, but military action demanded honest intelligence, limited objectives and an understanding of the consequences.

Three days before Trump launched Operation Epic Fury on Feb. 28, I warned in Fox News Digital that the administration needed to establish the facts before committing America to another Middle Eastern conflict. I never doubted that American forces could overwhelm Iran’s military. I doubted that Washington had a realistic plan for what came afterward. Eight months later, Washington still lacks a convincing answer, and the political consequences have become impossible to ignore.

The Fox News Voter Poll explains much of the Republican defeat. More than a third of voters called the Iran war crucial to their House vote, and about 6 in 10 said attacking Iran was the wrong decision.

FOX NEWS POLL: 71% THINK TRUMP ADMINISTRATION LACKS PLAN TO END IRAN WAR

In a separate Fox News survey, nearly twice as many preferred ending military involvement to lower gasoline prices as favored renewed attacks to stop Iran's nuclear program. That finding should trouble the White House. Americans did not necessarily dismiss the Iranian threat. Many simply concluded that the costs of confronting it had become too high.

The costs are staggering. A Pentagon estimate submitted to Congress put war spending at $47.1 billion through Oct. 16, a figure that excludes repairs to damaged American bases. As I documented Nov. 4, investigations by the Associated Press and The Wall Street Journal exposed extensive damage to American installations throughout the Middle East. The Journal put the repair bill at $5 billion to $15 billion. Congress must determine what was lost, whether some losses were preventable and what restoring our defenses will cost.

COST OF IRAN WAR EXPLODES AS TOLL ON US AIR FLEET NEARLY DOUBLES

Then there is the opportunity cost.

In August, I examined the Pentagon's decision to divert the Japan-based USS George Washington from the Pacific to the Middle East. That decision reduced America's carrier presence in a region where China poses our greatest long-term military challenge. A carrier committed to confronting Iran is unavailable for operations in the western Pacific. That is a strategic tradeoff Washington cannot afford to overlook.

TRUMP IS WINNING EVERY BATTLE IN IRAN—AND RISKING THE WAR THAT MATTERS

China remains America’s principal strategic competitor, and every commitment to Iran must be weighed against that reality.

In 1974, as a young lieutenant in South Korea, I served in then-Lt. Col. Colin Powell’s battalion. Powell later championed a doctrine that stressed clear objectives, overwhelming force, public support and an exit strategy. In my July Fox column, I questioned whether Washington was honoring those principles in Iran. Tuesday’s election exposed the consequences of neglecting one of them: A president cannot sustain a costly war indefinitely without the support of the American people.

AMERICANS 'FRUSTRATED' ABOUT IRAN WAR GOING INTO MIDTERMS AS TRUMP ADMIN HAS DECISION TO MAKE: GOP LAWMAKER

Instead of the short campaign Trump promised, America has spent eight months cycling through strikes, ceasefires and negotiations that have produced no durable settlement.

Iran has suffered enormously. The opening strikes killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei and devastated important military installations, yet the regime survives. Its nuclear ambitions remain unresolved and Tehran continues threatening commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Eight months of military punishment have weakened Iran, but they have not produced the durable settlement Americans were led to expect.

None of this counsels surrender to Tehran. America needs a strategy capable of achieving something more lasting than another round of destruction.

In January, Democrats can investigate military losses, demand testimony from Pentagon leaders, impose conditions on appropriations and challenge the administration’s authority to continue fighting. Trump retains considerable executive power, but congressional resistance could complicate nearly every national security initiative of his final two years.

Tehran is already celebrating. Iran's parliament speaker, Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf, declared that "Americans said NO TO WAR." That is precisely the conclusion Washington must not encourage. Beijing and Moscow will also be watching to see whether the Iran war has weakened America's ability to sustain its commitments elsewhere.

The day after the 2006 election, President George W. Bush announced that Rumsfeld would be replaced by Robert Gates. Two months later, he announced a new Iraq strategy built around a troop surge, and Gen. David Petraeus, whose counterinsurgency expertise I publicly supported, took command.

Trump may face similar pressure to replace Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth or other senior advisers. Their assessments of Iranian capabilities and protection of American forces deserve scrutiny. But new faces alone will accomplish little unless the president also rethinks the strategy itself.

The administration is already divided over what comes next. Axios reported that Vance and presidential envoy Steve Witkoff favor pursuing an agreement, while Hegseth and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu support renewed military action. Other senior advisers favor continued economic pressure. Trump must decide among those competing approaches, but only after establishing which one offers America a realistic prospect of lasting security.

Trump needs experienced advisers willing to challenge his assumptions, an honest accounting of the war’s costs and a fresh assessment of how closely American decisions should follow Israel’s preferences. Our interests overlap, but they are not identical.

Above all, he must decide what victory means. Is it preventing Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons, protecting regional shipping, negotiating a durable settlement or removing the regime? Those goals demand very different commitments, and Americans deserve to know which their president intends to pursue.

For now, Trump appears reluctant to resume major attacks while diplomatic efforts continue. That gives him an opportunity to reconsider his approach before another round of fighting imposes still greater costs. He should use it.

Twenty years ago, voters forced Washington to reconsider a costly war. They have delivered another warning.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

Iran’s rulers should not mistake the election for permission to threaten America. But Trump should not mistake battlefield superiority for a winning strategy.

Our troops have done what their country asked of them. Their commander in chief now owes them, and the American people, a credible plan to finish the mission at a price this country is willing to pay.

item.title: Uber removes driver after woman reports disturbing encounter during late-night ride
item.description: A rideshare expert weighs in after a 22-year-old woman opened up about a disturbing late-night Uber ride. She said the driver canceled while she was still in the car in Chicago.
item.content:encoded:
A young woman is warning other rideshare passengers after she says her Uber driver canceled a late-night trip while she was still inside the car.

Elyse Madrid, 22, said she and a friend ordered an Uber at about 2:30 a.m. on a recent Saturday to travel from Chicago's Belmont Cragin neighborhood to a karaoke bar, according to CBS News Chicago.

During the trip, Madrid noticed they did not appear to be heading in the right direction. Her concern grew when she said she watched the driver cancel the trip in the app while she and her friend were still sitting inside the vehicle.

WOMAN'S ROUTINE UBER RIDE TAKES ALARMING TURN AFTER HER DRIVER MISSES THE EXIT

Fox News Digital reached out to Madrid for comment.

Uber told Fox News Digital that the driver in question has been removed from the platform while the incident is being investigated.

"What has been reported is deeply distressing, and we have removed the driver's access to the Uber platform," an Uber spokesperson said. "We've reached out to police, and will support their investigation in any way we can."

Madrid said she confronted the driver. She said he blamed the cancellation on problems with his phone and at one point claimed his sister had canceled the trip.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

She demanded that he pull over and eventually got out of the vehicle with her friend on Randolph Street near the Kennedy Expressway, according to the same outlet. 

"When we got out the car, he sped off like in a panic," Madrid said.

She said the driver took off at about 40 to 50 mph. Madrid later filed a police report.

The experience was particularly troubling for Madrid, who said she had been assaulted in a cab the previous August.

Dillon Abend, the New Jersey-based founder and CEO of rideshare safety app 3rd-i, told Fox News Digital that passengers should speak up during a ride as soon as they notice something unusual.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES

"You do not want to stay silent," Abend said. "You do want to stand up for yourself and speak out."

If a driver cancels a trip while the passenger is still inside, Abend says a rider should stay calm, ask what happened and clearly state where the rider wants to be dropped off. 

If the driver does not cooperate or if the passenger believes there is an immediate threat, he said people should call 911 and alert a trusted friend or family member.

Abend also recommended that people share a live location with someone and check that the driver, vehicle and license plate match the information shown in the rideshare app before even getting inside.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Unexpected changes in direction can also be a warning sign. 

Abend said riders can use a separate mapping app to check whether they are still heading toward their destination if something seems off.

The incident comes about a month after another woman said her late-night Uber driver asked to stop at a parking garage to charge his electric vehicle before missing an exit, Fox News Digital previously reported.

That passenger ultimately ended the trip and contacted police. 

Uber told Fox News Digital at the time that it investigated the report and took appropriate action.

item.title: Pierce Brosnan backs 'Fantastic Beasts' star for next James Bond, predicts fans will be 'blown away'
item.description: Pierce Brosnan singled out Callum Turner as a standout among the actors being considered for the next James Bond role in a Vanity Fair interview.
item.content:encoded:
Pierce Brosnan is throwing in his two cents into the conversation regarding who should be chosen to play the next James Bond, nearly 25 years after he last played the iconic character.

During a recent interview with Vanity Fair, the 73-year-old actor said he is following along with the public as "an audience member," adding he is just as "eager" as everyone else "to see who is going to play this epic role of cinematic history." He did however give one actor a special shout out.

"All the men who are on the list now are actors I admire," he said. "Callum, Callum Turner is someone I’ve worked with, and he’s so strong. They all have a voice and a physique, and a presence on film. They all have longevity as actors, all of these young men."

While he doesn't know who will take on the iconic role next, Brosnan wishes whoever is chosen "the very best of life and strength and courage."

FORMER BOND GIRL SAYS NEXT 007 SHOULD BE 'ANOTHER GORGEOUS MAN' AS JAMES BOND DECISION

Brosnan first appeared as agent 007 in the 1995 movie, "GoldenEye," having taken over the reigns from Timothy Dalton. He appeared in his final Bond movie in 2002 with the release of "Die Another Day," and was replaced by Daniel Craig in the 2006 movie, "Casino Royale."

Craig starred as James Bond in six films, before hanging up his badge following the release of "No Time to Die" in 2021.

"You know, it’s hard to tell who it would be, but I eagerly await to hear the news and the celebration of the next James Bond," Brosnan said.

In addition to a new actor playing Bond, the film is also getting a new director in Denis Villeneuve, who will be taking over the franchise, which excites Brosnan.

"I think we are going to be blown away. I really do. [Villeneuve] is such an iconoclastic director. His work is visionary, and his stealth and imagination of camera work and storytelling is so visceral and sensuous," he said. "It’s going to be great. It’s going to be truly magnificent."

When speaking with GQ about the mental and physical load of playing the character in September 2022, he nonchalantly explained, "You get chipped, you get nicked, you pull muscles, you get stitched up."

He also spoke to the outlet about his own approach to playing James Bond, saying he "was trying to walk a line between Roger [Moore] and Sean Connery," who played the role before him, and "not being shy about taking from their work."

"I allowed myself the grace to try and get the sense of humour that both men brought to the part," he said.

Brosnan recently told Fox News Digital that he warned his sons that Hollywood is "a very tough business" that requires discipline, adding that he believes his sons are capable of handling it.

His youngest son Paris, 25, recently made his feature film debut in the movie, "Seniors," alongside John Rhys-Davies. His son Dylan, 29, is now also stepping into the entertainment industry, starring in an ad campaign with Brosnan for the 170th anniversary for Burberry.

"I was with my son, Dylan Thomas Brosnan, which was just absolutely wonderful, and we had the most magnificent time," he said about working with his son. "I’d never seen so many people on a set in all my days for such an event. Everybody was very charming."

item.title: Rory McIlroy defends Scottie Scheffler amid lazy criticisms about World No 1's non-global schedule
item.description: Rory McIlroy defends Scottie Scheffler against critics who say the world No. 1 should travel more, calling it his prerogative as a family man.
item.content:encoded:
Scottie Scheffler is the best golfer on Earth and has been recognized as such for 176 consecutive weeks. Being the No. 1-ranked player in the world for more than three years running comes with a spotlight, and with a spotlight comes criticism. What makes Scheffler different than most who have ever been in his position is that he doesn't care about the spotlight, not even a little bit.

Scheffler boasts about the fact that golf does not define him and that the game falls well below both his faith and young family on the list of most important things in his life. If you were to ask either a golf fan or even his peers to describe Scheffler, most would say he's a very normal person who loves spending time with his family, who also happens to be a generational talent with a golf club in his hand.

These circumstances, coupled with his style of play where he'll ball-strike his opponents to death, have led to his biggest criticism being that he is simply 'boring.' In recent months, however, some of the criticism's focus has turned to his playing schedule.

SCOTTIE SCHEFFLER SHARES A PERFECTLY IMPERFECT ASSESSMENT OF WORK-LIFE BALANCE, THE CHALLENGES OF FATHERHOOD

In September, Golf Monthly published a column claiming that Scheffler has an obligation to travel the world and be a "global ambassador" for the game as the world No. 1.

"One thing he absolutely should be criticised for, though, is the fact he’s seemingly allergic to leaving America for more than a fortnight each year," the column stated, after noting that he is not trying to be someone he isn't.

The 30-year-old made 20 starts during the 2026 PGA Tour season, with just the Scottish Open and Open Championship taking place outside of the United States. He won three times, earning just shy of $31 million.

The timing of the story coming in the fall, with Scheffler already in the midst of his "offseason," led to a discussion about whether or not he did have a responsibility to play all around the world, and it has continued all the way into November.

RORY MCILROY FIRES BACK AT KEVIN KISNER AFTER 'DOGS---' COMMENT ABOUT GROWING THE GAME

The topic has even reached Rory McIlroy's orbit, and the six-time major champion believes anyone saying Scheffler needs to travel the world more is wrong.

item.title: The cast of 'Madden' hits the red carpet to talk about whether they've chowed down on turducken
item.description: The "Madden" movie cast, including Nicolas Cage and Christian Bale, faced the ultimate John Madden question at the premiere: have you had turducken?
item.content:encoded:
The new movie "Madden" is about to take the world by storm — it remains to be seen if that's because it's good or because ... well, that it's not — and so the cast of it has been hit with the biggest John Madden-related question there is.

Have you ever had a turducken?

If you're unaware of what a turducken is (where the hell have you been), it's the unholy Thanksgiving sin against nature that is a chicken stuffed inside a duck, which is, in turn, crammed inside of a turkey that Madden made popular.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

I've never had one myself. Not because I'm against it — I'm staunchly pro-turducken — but I've simply never been given he chance to score a poultry hat trick.

Maybe that's because I never got to be in a movie about John Madden, patron saint of turducken, as these folks have.

First we've got Christian Bale, who plays Al Davis in the movie. When he's not berating people on set, he's preaching the finer points of food safety. Probably smart to dive into the world of turducken with a movie prop that has been sitting out for more than half the day.

Next was Nicolas Cage, who plays John Madden himself (no, seriously). He didn't answer the question, but said he did get a lot of turducken on his hand chopping one up the way Madden used to. I'm sure he has eaten weirder foods crammed inside of each other before, so a turducken is probably not a big deal to him.

Super Bowl champion Julian Edelman was at the film's premiere and said that he has never had it, but always wanted one of the ones Madden mangled with his bare hands every Thanksgiving.

And, finally, we have the lovely Sienna Miller, who plays Carol Sagal Davis, and finally we have a cast member who has actually eaten turducken. She said that she and co-star Kathryn Hahn (who plays Virginia Madden) helped themselves to some backup turducken.

item.title: Cowboys star Brandon Aubrey details journey from soccer player to software engineer to Pro Bowl kicker
item.description: Brandon Aubrey went from MLS and USL soccer to software engineering before his wife pushed him to pursue NFL kicking with the Dallas Cowboys.
item.content:encoded:
Brandon Aubrey has become one of the best kickers in the NFL with the Dallas Cowboys, but his road to stardom has been far from linear.

Aubrey, 31, first played professional soccer in Major League Soccer (MLS) and then the United Soccer League (USL) before hanging up the spikes.

"I wasn't ready to retire from soccer, but when I looked around at the environment, I didn't perform as well as I needed to stick on a roster and I got cut a couple of times. And at that point, there wasn't a whole lot of money in soccer at the second tier. So, I slipped from the MLS into the USL," Aubrey told OutKick in a recent interview.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

"I had to really take a long, hard look at it, see if it was worth pursuing, and I could make triple the money I was making in that league as a software engineer, which my degree was in."

Aubrey said he had just gotten married to his wife, Jenn, and didn’t want to set his family back , so into software engineering he went. However, working as a software engineer wasn’t very fun for Aubrey.

Aubrey said that Jenn had a good, stable job and pushed him to pursue a career as an NFL kicker.

"With that support and a lot of hard work and commitment we were able to shift over towards being a kicker, and got a job in the USFL and eventually got noticed at the NFL level and was able to get a job here," Aubrey said.

Aubrey is in his fourth season with the Cowboys and has made the Pro Bowl in each of his first three seasons. He has made 127 of his 146 field-goal attempts with a long of 65 yards, while nailing 146 of 151 extra points.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

One of his 127 made field goals stands out more than the rest.

The New York Giants had gone up 37-34 in Week 2 of the 2025 season with just 25 seconds left in the game. It looked like the Cowboys were going to go 0-2 to start the year.

"They just put the dagger in us where they scored a long touchdown. to Nabers and he did the night-night celebration," Aubrey said. "We had like 12 seconds to go get 10 yards, got it and then we were in field-goal position and that's still a pretty coin-flippy field goal, maybe even less than a coin flip for historical statistics."

While a 64-yard field goal to tie the game might seem like less than a coin flip for Aubrey, he made it look easy. He nailed the kick to force overtime.

"To be able to go and hit that one through the uprights was awesome," Aubrey said.

However, his day wasn’t done there. Aubrey made a 46-yard field goal as the clock expired in overtime to give the Cowboys a thrilling 40-37 win.

In the chaos of life, and in Aubrey’s case, multiple career changes, sometimes your smile can suffer. The Pro Bowl kicker said he didn’t take good care of his smile as an adult and credited Invisalign for helping him restore his confidence.

"If you smile, I think that shows a lot of your personality. And for me, I put a lot of time and effort into my smile as a as a young kid. I guess I could say my parents put that time and effort into it and it was in a good spot and then shift happens. I didn't take good enough care of it as a college athlete and a young adult and my smile shifted as well. I think Invisalign clear liners are a fantastic fit for me as I try to invest in my smile, my overall health, my confidence," Aubrey, who spoke on behalf of Invisalign, said.

"You look good, you feel good, you play good."

item.title: ELAINE PARKER: Democrat win is a wake-up call for Republicans, not a vote for socialism
item.description: Midterm elections sent a clear message on affordability, but Democrats would be wrong to interpret their victories as a mandate for socialism.
item.content:encoded:
The American people sent a clear message in Tuesday's midterm elections. But Democrats would be making a serious mistake if they interpreted their victories as an endorsement of socialism.

Voters weren't demanding bigger government. They wanted relief from the affordability crisis.

Republicans shouldn't dismiss the results as a typical midterm setback either. The coalition that delivered President Donald Trump the White House and Republican control of Congress in 2024 expected results.

MEHEK COOKE: REPUBLICANS FAILED THE AFFORDABILITY TEST. THIS IS HOW TO WIN VOTERS BACK

The voters who hired Republicans to fix the affordability crisis are now holding them accountable for failing to deliver.

Americans were tired of inflation, unaffordable housing and watching their paychecks buy less. They believed Republicans would make their lives better.

FOX NEWS POLL: SQUEEZED BY COSTS, FRUSTRATED VOTERS TURN TO THE DEMOCRATS

But somewhere between winning and governing, Republicans lost control of that message.

Trump had a legitimate argument for tariffs: rebuilding American manufacturing and bringing back jobs lost under decades of trade policies, including NAFTA, signed by President Bill Clinton. But Republicans never adequately explained the long-term benefits. Voters heard about tariffs while worrying about higher prices.

The same communications failure plagued the One Big Beautiful Bill.

Republicans made lower individual tax rates permanent, restored immediate expensing for qualifying business investments and prevented trillions in scheduled tax increases. Yet how many Americans could explain what that legislation actually did for them?

What good is passing legislation that helps working families and small businesses if you can't explain how it makes their lives better?

Healthcare was another squandered opportunity.

When enhanced COVID-19-era Obamacare subsidies expired, Republicans could have offered a serious affordability alternative built around price transparency, competition and consumer choice. Instead, they surrendered the conversation.

Healthcare is part of the affordability crisis. Families don't separate their mortgage, groceries, insurance premiums and deductibles into political categories. It all comes from the same paycheck.

Perhaps the biggest warning came from Hispanic voters.

Trump made historic gains in 2024 by speaking to their economic aspirations, entrepreneurial spirit and desire for safe communities.

Following Trump's 2024 victory, his pollster, John McLaughlin, observed that Republicans had rented the Hispanic vote and warned they needed to work to keep it.

Unfortunately, they acted as though they owned it.

FLORIDA CONGRESSMAN DIAGNOSES GOP'S BLUE TSUNAMI LOSSES: 'WE FAILED TO MAKE THEM THINK WE CARED ABOUT THEM'

Economic frustration drove much of the erosion in support, but immigration enforcement contributed. Trump promised to secure the border and prioritize dangerous criminals. Instead, broader enforcement created fear in Hispanic communities, including among those who supported stronger border security.

Republicans worked hard to win those voters in 2024 and then seemingly forgot what brought them into the Republican column. They failed to maintain that trust, much less expand it.

My home state of Florida should be a wake-up call.

Republicans can celebrate electing Byron Donalds as Florida's first Black governor and holding major statewide offices. But Donalds narrowly defeated David Jolly despite a roughly 1.5-million Republican voter-registration advantage.

That advantage provided a cushion against the national Democratic swing, not immunity from it. Those margins should concern Republican leaders.

Then there's the war with Iran.

Whatever the administration's strategic justification, it failed to make a compelling case to Americans already struggling financially. Voters saw higher gasoline prices without a clearly articulated reason for the conflict.

None of this gives Democrats a mandate to push socialist policies.

A vote against Republican performance isn't necessarily a vote for higher taxes, more government spending or expanded bureaucracy. Many of these same voters supported Trump just two years ago because they wanted a different economic direction.

Democrats have earned an opportunity to address affordability, not a blank check for an ideological agenda.

Republicans, meanwhile, need to reconnect their policies to the people they're supposed to serve. Lower taxes, stronger small businesses, affordable healthcare and greater economic opportunity remain a compelling agenda. But voters need to see and feel the benefits.

Tuesday's election was not a mandate for socialism. It was a demand for affordability, accountability and results.

Americans did not suddenly change what they wanted. They changed whom they trusted to deliver it.

And unless both parties understand that distinction, they risk learning the same lesson all over again.

item.title: High school athlete cursed out by Seattle Storm owner runs against trans athlete at state championship
item.description: Ahnaleigh Wilson ran through a bone stress injury at the Pasco, WA state cross country finals, lining up against the Camas transgender athlete.
item.content:encoded:
It was a cross-country course filled with twists, turns, hills and switchbacks. There was nothing round about it. But for Eastmont High junior Ahnaleigh Wilson, this was a case of things coming full circle.

More than two years ago, Wilson finished second to a trans athlete in a Junior Olympic track race. That set her on a path of speaking out against biological boys competing in girls' sports. If her name looks familiar, it's because she's the one Seattle Storm co-owner Celeste Keaton cursed out at a WNBA game in July for holding a sign reading, "Thank You Sophie (Cunningham) For Speaking Up For Girls!"

It brought a high school girl to tears, but as you'll learn, it takes a lot more than that to stop Ahnaleigh.

SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM FAN WHO WAS CONFRONTED BY STORM CO-OWNER OPENS UP ON INCIDENT AND FACING TRANS ATHLETES

Since Keaton's tirade, quite a bit has happened in the world of Washington state transgender athletes. For the last month and a half, a male runner from Camas High who switched to the girls team midseason has dominated the headlines. After opening the season 76th in a boys' JV race, he crossed over to win a varsity girls' meet and knock female runners out of regional and state qualifying spots.

Well, guess who was lined up against him in Saturday's 4A girls state finals at Sun Willows Golf Course? That's right — one Ahnaleigh Wilson.

Wilson racing was no guarantee. Not just because she'd considered taking a stand against having to compete against a boy, but because she had a bone stress injury in her right fibula she feared might develop into a fracture. Her parents encouraged her not for health reasons. She didn't listen.

"I worked really hard this season, and I mean, I like running. So I wanted to run. I wanted to try at least," Wilson said.

It might have been good social-media material for activists had Wilson walked off in protest, but that wasn't going to happen. Plus, she'd already done enough in that department — regularly speaking in defense of girls and women despite her relatively shy nature.

She'd survived all the emotional abuse her detractors had thrown her way. Saturday was about surviving the physical.

BIOLOGICAL MALE COMPETING IN GIRLS' CROSS-COUNTRY RACE DENIES ANOTHER RUNNER AND HER TEAM A TRIP TO STATE

A healthy Wilson likely would have finished somewhere in the top third of Saturday's 155-girl field. Her usual time of 19:30 would have been good for 49th place. But this was not a healthy Wilson. This was a high school junior slogging through a 5000-meter course with searing pain every other step.

Ahnaleigh said she thought about quitting multiple times mid-race. But the cheers from the crowd kept her going. And we aren't talking about the ones from her parents, friends or coaches. We're talking about random supporters who knew her name because of everything she'd fought for.

"There were a few times I didn't know if I was going to finish, and I heard people I didn't recognize their voices, but there were people cheering for me, and that was really cool," she said.

Wilson's final time? 22:58.30 — which placed her 150th. The Camas male, meanwhile, finished 23rd, which wasn't fast enough to put him on the podium reserved for the top 16 runners.

This was his first race since Tuesday's election, when Washington voters decisively passed Initiative 638, which will enforce the separation of biological boys and girls in K-12 sports once it takes effect. And even though many runners at Saturday's race were relieved the measure got through, they were still motivated to outrun the boy in the girls race.

One was Skyview High runner Charlie Garrett, who, alongside teammate Sierra Retzlaff, walked off the start line in protest of the Camas runner last month. She'd heard that the boy told his teammates that his goal was to beat them every time since that act, and while he was successful in doing so Saturday (Garrett and Retzlaff finished 39th and 92nd, respectively), Garrett took solace in the fact that she wouldn't have to face him again.

WASHINGTON HS GIRLS BLAST MALE ATHLETE PARTICIPATING IN TRACK MEET: 'DON'T THINK THAT THAT'S RIGHT OR FAIR'

"I guess the motivation (to beat him) is just that I don't want my spot to be taken away by someone who shouldn't be in my race. That's my main motivation" said Garrett, a junior. "I didn't do it this season — and I won't have to this season. But I mean, me and my mom are very competitive people, so I think it just runs in the blood to try and do better than the person who's causing us stress."

Echoing that sentiment was Kamiakin High sophomore Lauren Baumann.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

"My goal was to beat the guy from Camas because I don't think he should be racing in a girls race," said Baumann, who finished 11 spots behind him. "When he passed me at the 800 and I tried to stay with him but couldn't, it made me feel really really mad and just that I couldn't do anything to stop it. But I'm glad that he won't be able to run next year."

I-638 could go into effect as soon as December 3, although there may be legal challenges delaying its implementation. But girls such as Wilson, Garrett and Retzlaff — all of whom played critical roles in getting it passed — are taking their metaphorical victory laps.

That said, perhaps nobody was as emotional Saturday as Ahnaleigh's mom, Elizabeth, who broke down in tears after her daughter's race.

"I can't believe she went out and did that with a bone stress...that's just heart," Elizabeth said. "She started this journey racing a boy, and she ended it, and hopefully this will be the last time a boy competes against girls."

X-rays will reveal whether Ahnaleigh — who was limping after the race — has a stress fracture. But she proved something Saturday. Whether it's a state cross country race or a ballot initiative — no matter how painful, she is going to finish what she started.

item.title: Gulf War veteran left homeless after heart surgery details how he rebuilt his life from 'square one'
item.description: Gulf War veteran Thomas Garrett Jr. shares his fight to rebuild his life after heart surgery as Fox Corporation and U.S.VETS partner on the "Make Camo Your Cause" campaign.
item.content:encoded:
Gulf War veteran Thomas Garrett Jr. returned home to celebratory parades, but years later, he found himself homeless after undergoing heart surgery.

Garrett’s efforts to rebuild his life after becoming homeless are highlighted in Fox Corporation’s sixth annual "Make Camo Your Cause" campaign with U.S.VETS, a nationwide initiative ahead of Veterans Day aimed at helping end veteran homelessness.

"The homecoming was a phenomenal event," Garrett said Saturday on "Fox News Live."

"I became homeless after having heart surgery. So that changed everything about my dynamic in life," he added.

AMERICA'S WOUNDED, STRUGGLING VETERANS GET BRAND-NEW HOMES BUILT BY FLORIDA TEENS

U.S.VETS, a national nonprofit dedicated to ending veteran homelessness, provides housing, food and career help to service members in need. According to the organization, it assists more than 20,000 veterans and their families each year. To date, U.S.VETS has served over 500,000 meals, provided 418,000 nights of shelter and placed 3,000 veterans into permanent housing.

Quandrea Patterson, executive director of U.S.VETS, explained that Garrett’s experience reflects a broader challenge facing veterans as they transition from military to civilian life.

NEW YORK JETS OWNER WOODY JOHNSON TO BE HONORED AT TUNNEL TO TOWERS GALA FOR DECADE-LONG PARTNERSHIP

"A lot of times when veterans are in service, they're told, and they know exactly what to do because they're mission-focused," Patterson said. "And then during that transition from active service to civilian service or veteran status, a lot of the information, a lot of the things to expect are unknown."

The uncertainty surrounding that transition can leave veterans vulnerable to homelessness, Patterson said. 

For Garrett, U.S.VETS offered the structure and support he needed to move forward.

"U.S.VETS is a new starting point for veterans," Garrett said. "It's a square one to where you can build up your life the way the veteran themselves need it. It gives us good structure. It gives us a good routine to begin and to build from there."

TRUMP PROMOTES FREEDOM HAULERS INITIATIVE TO FAST-TRACK MILITARY VETERANS INTO TRUCKING JOBS

Ahead of Veterans Day, Patterson stressed that honoring those who served requires more than celebrating them once a year.

"Freedom isn’t free, and for the freedom that we're experiencing, that, there is somebody out there volunteering to put their life on the line and to navigate the unknown," Patterson said. "When they get out, we should wrap our arms around them to make sure that they know that that service was appreciated in more than just words, but in deed as well."

item.title: Blue Angels pilot removed from team for 'failing to uphold' standards, Navy says
item.description: Blue Angels pilot Scott Laux was removed for failing to uphold team standards, forcing the squadron to fly five jets at its Pensacola season finale.
item.content:encoded:
A Blue Angels pilot was removed from the Navy’s flight demonstration team for "failing to uphold" its standards, leaving squadron with a five-jet show on Friday.

The dismissal comes just months after a controversial low Pensacola Beach flyover in July that sent debris flying, raising concern for public safety.

Maj. Scott Laux, a second-year member of the elite team, was identified as Blue Angel No. 6. The Chief of Naval Air Training (CNATRA) confirmed his removal to the Pensacola News Journal, saying the decision was announced Friday before the season finale at home in Pensacola.

NAVY SAYS NO REPRIMANDS OR FIRINGS AFTER BLUE ANGELS’ LOW PASS OVER BEACHGOERS

"Blue Angel #6 was removed from the team for failing to uphold the standards expected of members of the Navy Flight Demonstration Squadron and will not participate in the team’s remaining performance this season," Chief of Naval Air Training (CNATRA) public affairs office wrote in a statement Friday.

When reached for comment, CNATRA noted Sunday the removal came Nov. 3.

Laux previously defended the team’s low-flying displays after the July flyover over Pensacola Beach sent tents, beach chairs and umbrellas flying as sand swept across the shoreline.

"We appreciate the trust in support and it’s our privilege to be able to perform in that way," Laux told Rolling with Madrina after the incident. "We’re gonna keep bringing the heat and continue doing it safely."

VIRAL VIDEO OF JETS BUZZING DHL STADIUM IN CAPE TOWN PROMPTS AVIATION SAFETY INVESTIGATION

Navy and War Department leaders had previously defended the low flyovers.

"Flight debrief complete. No reprimands. No firings. No problem," Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao wrote on X in July. "That’s the sound of Freedom! Semper fi and Hooyah."

War Secretary Pete Hegseth had vowed more support.

"The flyovers will continue until morale improves," Hegseth wrote on X.

The White House posted a photo meme of the controversial flyover from its official X account.

"It's okay to love America," the post read.

HEGSETH STEPS IN TO ‘FIX’ SITUATION AFTER APACHE PILOTS SUSPENDED FOR ‘SALUTE FROM THE SHORES’ FLYOVER

The Navy has not said when Laux was dismissed or what conduct prompted the decision. His photo and biography are no longer featured on the Blue Angels’ website's team page.

Laux was absent from the squadron’s NAS Pensacola Homecoming Air Show on Friday and Saturday, where the team performed with five jets instead of its usual six. Laux's role was the opposing solo, which flies with lead solo #5 in the head-on crossing passes and mirror-image maneuvers that fill the gaps between the four-jet Diamond’s routines.

The routines were adjusted to account for the missing jet, according to reports.

The 2026 narrator, Lt. Commander Ronny Hafeza, might replace Laux on the 2027 team. The Blue Angels officers serve three-year terms, one as a narrator as Laux did.

Laux, a native of Chantilly, Va., graduated from the U.S. Naval Academy in 2012 with a degree in Chinese and earned his wings in 2015, according to his bio, which as of Sunday morning could still be accessed on the site despite no longer being listed with the rest of the team. He later transitioned to the F-35C Lightning II and served as an instructor pilot before joining the Blue Angels in September 2024. Before becoming Blue Angels #6, he served as the show's narrator.

Laux has more than 1,300 flight hours and 169 aircraft carrier landings. His awards include two Navy and Marine Corps Commendation Medals and multiple unit awards.

item.title: DAVID MARCUS: How Ashley Moody survived the blue tsunami and emerged as a GOP star.
item.description: Ashley Moody defied the blue tsunami to hold Florida's Senate seat, and her rapid rise in GOP seniority could reshape the Republican future.
item.content:encoded:
Even in the face of massive losses in last week’s Midterm elections, Republicans had a few winners, and none may have longer-lasting effects than Sen. Ashley Moody of Florida who defied national trends for a GOP hold in the Sunshine State.

Going into Tuesday’s contests, holding a Senate seat in Florida may have seemed like the least Republicans could do, but it turned out to be a night where the least they could do was the most they did, and those who did win should be learned from.

"I fought tooth and nail this election to make sure Floridians know that what we have here is special, and it can be dismantled in one cycle," Moody told Fox News Digital in the wake of the blue tsunami, and while that message faltered in states like Texas, in Florida it stuck.

FLORIDA CONGRESSMAN DIAGNOSES GOP'S BLUE TSUNAMI LOSSES: 'WE FAILED TO MAKE THEM THINK WE CARED ABOUT THEM'

Moody said her campaign held to two basic messages.

"Talking to folks on the ground and meeting them where they were was vital, and I heard many people from all political backgrounds present a consistent message – they want a government that is accountable and a government that protects their pursuit of the American Dream. I put that front and center in my campaign and Floridians backed me for it."

Accountability and the American dream: These are two very good places to start as the GOP licks its wounds and seeks a path back to power on Capitol Hill having squandered both houses in this cycle.

DESANTIS CALLS GOP MIDTERM LOSSES 'EXTINCTION-LEVEL EVENT' — AND EXPLAINS WHY FLORIDA SURVIVED

Many have been tempted to dismiss Moody’s victory by saying, "but it's red Florida." But red Texas turned bluer than the Gulf of America. So no, Florida did not carry Ashley Moody. Ashley Moody helped carry Florida.

Moody was twice elected statewide as attorney general, first in 2018 by low single digits, then in 2022 by a whopping 21% of the vote, and unlike Ken Paxton, the Texas AG who lost his Senate bid last week, Moody did not have a long resume of scandal to bog her down.

Moody also outperformed South Carolina Sen. Darlene Graham, who took over the seat of her late brother Lindsey Graham after he died earlier this year, a decision driven by President Donald Trump that many believe cost Republicans the Palmetto state seat.

Now, in the new Congress, Republicans will end up having lost between seven and nine seats. What this means for Moody is a fast track to seniority. With GOP Senate stalwarts like John Cornyn of Texas and Susan Collins of Maine having lost this cycle, Moody has jumped significantly ahead in line.

MASSIVE UPSET: ANDREWS DOWNS TRUMP-BACKED GRAHAM IN RUBY-RED SOUTH CAROLINA

Although Moody is just as much responsible for Republican success in Florida - which also included the election of Rep. Byron Donalds as governor - as Republican success in Florida is for Moody, one would be remiss not to mention current Gov. Ron DeSantis, the architect of the so-called ‘free state of Florida."

DeSantis has built a GOP brand in Florida that is laser focused on the two issues Moody credited for her victory, government accountability and saving the American dream for the next generation.

DeSantis made his state a beacon for conservatives across America who came in droves from places like New York City, now, it may become a lighthouse, guiding a national Republican Party adrift at sea back to the shores of electoral victory.

Of the GOP wipeout, DeSantis said, "A lot of our voters who stayed home, they stayed home because they were frustrated with the lack of productivity from Republicans in the House and Senate. That’s just a fact. They were promised big things, and they didn’t deliver it."

This is noticeably at odds with Vice President JD Vance’s theory of the loss, which states that GOP voters did in fact come out, but voted for Democrats, mainly because of the war in Iran and our nation’s relationship with Israel.

Figuring out which of these theories is true, or at least dominant, is the first order of business for Republicans looking to regroup, and it is worth noting that while the GOP lost Vance’s old Senate seat in Ohio, Moody held Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s Florida seat intact.

Vance and DeSantis may get the chance to pitch their visions of the GOP to Americans over the next two years in a presidential primary race, but in the meantime, the biggest Republican winner of the Midterm debacle is Ashley Moody, who suddenly looks like a force in American politics that we should all get used to.

item.title: Houston Texans and Los Angeles Chargers meet in a matchup of two surprisingly struggling NFL teams

Stadiums are used for a lot of things, and planning for events and games can’t be easy. Sometimes they provide flex schedule games so that they can put bigger and better games in prime spots.

The Houston Texans come into this game with a 2-5 record, but if you’re going to pick either of these two teams to make the postseason, it is hard to pick against Houston. item.title: MICHAEL GUILLEN: Science's fantastic discoveries are making religion more credible
item.description: Dark matter and dark energy account for 95% of the cosmos, meaning science is based on only 5% of what's real, deepening the universe's mystery.
item.content:encoded:
I’ll never forget the time I received my very own microscope for Christmas; suddenly, a drop of pond water became a teeming cosmos of strange, wriggling creatures. Nor will I ever forget peering through my first telescope; suddenly, the moon’s eerie, cratered surface exploded to life and looked close enough for me to touch.

Those two boyhood experiences tell the entire, exciting, unexpected story of science in a nutshell. With every new, more powerful imaging device, scientists have gradually, spectacularly brought to light the once-shrouded secrets of the microscopic and macroscopic cosmos.

Throughout this long, impressive eye-opening drama, scientists have justifiably boasted about how their discoveries are systematically ridding our species of its hoary, benighted superstitions, religion included. This conceit is displayed in the title of Carl Sagan’s book The Demon-Haunted World: Science As a Candle in the Dark. For Carl — a professor of mine at Cornell — science was indeed the great, bright hope for a terribly dim-witted world.

NASA'S CHANDRA TELESCOPE REVEALS MILKY WAY'S OUTER REACHES MAY STRETCH FARTHER THAN PREVIOUSLY KNOWN

But, the story of science hasn’t turned out as the optimists prophesied, not by a long shot. That’s because modern science is discovering there’s far, far more to reality than meets the eye, than even our most sensitive instruments can see. That we live in a demon-haunted cosmos after all — one infested with invisible, inscrutable spirits with such names as dark matter and dark energy.

As a grad student at Cornell, I recall learning about what my astronomy professors called the "missing mass problem," a mystery dating back to 1933, when Swiss astronomer Fritz Zwicky used data from Mount Wilson Observatory’s powerful Hooker telescope to study clusters of galaxies. To his astonishment, Zwicky discovered that galaxies are swarming within each cluster like bees in a hive at a much faster clip than conventional physics can explain.

NEIL DEGRASSE TYSON DARES GOVERNMENT TO 'JUST SHOW THE ALIEN,' AS DISCLOSURE FERVOR CONTINUES TO GROW

In class, I learned that these clustered galaxies would need to have roughly ten times more mass to explain their unusual swiftness. This means that most of the galaxies’ collective mass is "missing" — is invisible to us. Zwicky called this ghostly mass "dunkle materie," German for dark matter.

Scientists today offer many fanciful, high-brow explanations for dark matter, but the plain truth is that, nearly a century after Zwicky’s discovery, we still have no idea whatsoever what it is. For now, the consensus is that, like conventional matter, dunkle materie is gravitational in nature — which is why it can tug on and speed up the clustered galaxies. But, very unlike conventional matter, dunkle materie does not radiate or reflect light — which is why it’s invisible.

FROM COCKROACH MILK TO STEPPING ON SNAKES, IG NOBEL AWARDS CELEBRATES SCIENCE AT ITS ODDEST

It wasn’t the first time data from the powerful Hooker telescope near Pasadena, California, delivered a scientific bombshell. Back in 1929 American lawyer-turned-astronomer Edwin Hubble used that very same instrument to discover that the universe is expanding. Thereafter, astronomers simply assumed the expansion was slowing down, owing to the universe’s collective gravity putting the brakes on it.

But, in 1998, the story of science took yet another startling turn to the dark side, when two separate teams of astronomers discovered that the expansion of our universe is actually speeding up, not slowing down. This implies the existence of an invisible, inscrutable, repulsive "something" that permeates the whole of our universe.

At a 1998 symposium at the Australian Academy of Science in Canberra, University of Chicago cosmologist Michael Turner gave the "something" a name: dark energy. But giving the phantom material a name doesn’t explain it. To this day, as with dark matter, dark energy remains a complete mystery — notwithstanding the countless published but unsupported attempts to explain it.

The discoveries of dark matter and dark energy would rate little more than a sensational footnote in the impressive story arc of science were it not for one very inconvenient truth. Today, scientists reckon that, all told, the two shadowy spirits account for ninety-five percent of the observable cosmos (never mind the existence of the totally unobservable cosmos beyond the Cosmic Horizon). Ninety-five percent!

DR MARC SIEGEL: I WENT LOOKING FOR MIRACLES AFTER OCT. 7. I FOUND ANGELS HIDING IN PLAIN SIGHT

It means that what we see — even with our most powerful, most sophisticated imaging devices — is only five percent of what’s actually "out there." Which means the whole of science — all its experiments, all its theories, the entirety of what it claims to understand about our demon-haunted world — is based on a measly five percent of what’s real. The other ninety-five percent of what exists remains a complete mystery.

This, in turn, means that, far from demystifying the universe, the twisting, turning story of science is actually mystifying the universe in ways that make religion more credible, not less.

The more secrets of the macroscopic and microscopic cosmos science brings to light, the more we discover how very, very, very little we understand about reality.

The more brightly Sagan’s "candle in the dark" burns, the more it reveals the truth of the Apostle Paul’s words, stated nearly 2,000 years ago: "For now we see through a glass, darkly."

item.title: Restaurants bring back old-school hospitality as nostalgia takes hold across America
item.description: Ford's Garage president Billy Downs built his hospitality training program around his grandmother's warmth as restaurant chains rediscover nostalgia.
item.content:encoded:
After years of modernization, restaurant chains are rediscovering the appeal of the past.

Pizza Hut has revisited its classic red-roof dining experience, while Cracker Barrel faced backlash over efforts to modernize its familiar image.

Across the industry, nostalgia has become a way to reconnect with consumers who still have an affinity for the restaurants they remember. But as chains revisit vintage decor, familiar branding and throwback menus, some restaurant operators see an opportunity to revive something less tangible: old-fashioned hospitality.

DISCONTINUED CRACKER BARREL FOODS THAT FANS ARE BEGGING TO GET BACK

At Ford's Garage, a 36-unit casual-dining chain modeled after a 1920s service station, Billy Downs has turned to an unlikely source of inspiration for the company's hospitality training program: his grandmother.

"We designed a training program that was designed after what a 'Greatest Generation' grandma would have served their family," the Michigan-based Ford's Garage president told Fox News Digital.

The program, dubbed the "hospitality wheel," draws on the warmth and personal attention Downs remembers from visiting his grandmother, an approach the company hopes to replicate across its growing restaurant footprint.

"I'll tell you this, she made you feel special, and that's what we want people to come out of this is feel special when they go to a Ford's Garage," Downs said.

KFC UNVEILS RADICALLY DIFFERENT RESTAURANT IN MAJOR COMEBACK PUSH

That philosophy extends beyond the training program. Downs said the chain places considerable emphasis on making guests feel welcome and fostering personal connections.

"We also know that we have a unique dining experience in terms of the environment, but we want to have that hospitality be really important and we want people to get connected when they come on in," he said.

That emphasis on personal connection comes as the restaurant industry increasingly embraces technology and automation, raising questions about the role of human interaction in the dining experience.

Chef Joe Isidori, owner of Arthur & Sons, which has locations in New York and Florida, believes that as technology becomes more prevalent, the human element of hospitality could become an increasingly valuable commodity.
